Benchmarking Vendor-Guided Optimizations on
Edge NPUs: From NPU Only to End-to-End
Performance

Abstract. Edge NPU performance depends not only on hardware ca-
pabilities, but also on model transformation and the overall deployment
pipeline. We propose a benchmarking methodology that separates these
effects by comparing three configurations: Baseline, Vendor Guided NPU
Only (VG-NPU), and Vendor Guided End-to-End (VG-E2E), where VG-
NPU preserves common model I/O and host-side processing while VG-
E2E follows the vendor-native deployment pipeline. We apply this method-
ology to four edge NPUs and three vision workloads. VG-NPU improves
both accuracy and runtime-call latency in 10 of 12 NPU–workload com-
binations, whereas VG-E2E reduces System-level latency in all combina-
tions but improves accuracy in only four. Moreover, NPU-level perfor-
mance rankings do not always match End-to-End rankings, and VG-
E2E provides an additional 10.4–70.7% reduction in System-level la-
tency over VG-NPU. These results demonstrate the importance of eval-
uating vendor-guided optimization separately at the controlled model-
transformation and full deployment levels.

Keywords: Edge NPU · Benchmarking · Vendor-Guided Optimization
· Inference Performance · End-to-End Evaluation

1 Introduction

As AI deployment expands, efficient inference has become increasingly impor-
tant, particularly in mobile and edge environments with tight power and resource
constraints. Neural Processing Units (NPUs) address this demand by accelerat-
ing tensor operations commonly used in neural networks, often providing higher
efficiency than general-purpose CPUs and GPUs for supported workloads [13].
In practice, however, NPU inference performance depends not only on hard-
ware compute capability, but also on the surrounding software stack, including
operator support, compiler optimizations, quantization, runtime execution, and
input/output processing.

Evaluating NPU-based inference systems requires considering both accuracy
and latency. Accuracy reflects how well the predictive quality of the original
model is preserved during deployment to an NPU, while latency measures the
execution time required to produce the final prediction from an input. In particu-
lar, latency can differ substantially depending on whether it measures only NPU
inference or end-to-end execution including preprocessing and postprocessing.
This study focuses on how accuracy and latency change across the deployment
pipelines of different NPUs.


Comparing different NPUs fairly is challenging. NPUs differ not only in hard-
ware architecture and supported operators, but also in their compilers, quantiza-
tion policies, precision settings, runtime interfaces, and preprocessing/postprocessing
pipelines. Consequently, even when starting from the same source model, apply-
ing vendor-recommended model transformations and deployment recipes can
change not only the final executable model, but also which operations are exe-
cuted on the NPU and how the overall deployment pipeline is constructed. As
a result, comparing only the final end-to-end (E2E) performance reported for
each vendor makes it difficult to determine whether an observed performance
difference arises from model transformations performed for NPU execution or
from the broader deployment pipeline, including preprocessing, postprocessing,
and runtime overheads.


Prior work has proposed benchmarking methodologies and evaluation met-
rics for fair comparison of ML inference systems [13, 12], and has analyzed how
preprocessing, postprocessing, framework, and runtime overheads beyond model
inference affect end-to-end performance [11, 4]. Other studies have shown that
the execution performance of the same model can vary depending on quan-
tization, compilers, deployment tools, and hardware-specific optimizations [7,
1]. However, these studies have primarily focused on cross-platform comparison,
system-level overheads, or the effects of individual optimization techniques. They
have not explicitly separated the effect of vendor-guided optimization into two
levels: model transformation under fixed model inputs, outputs, and host-side
processing, and actual vendor-native end-to-end deployment. By distinguishing
these two levels, this study separately examines how model transformation and
full deployment affect accuracy and latency.


To investigate this research gap, we define three experimental conditions:
Baseline, Vendor-Guided NPU-Only (VG-NPU), and Vendor-Guided End-to-
End (VG-E2E). Baseline serves as a reference configuration that permits only
the transformations required for NPU execution while limiting optional vendor-
specific optimizations. VG-NPU applies the vendor-guided model transforma-
tion recipe while preserving the same model inputs and outputs and the same
host-side processing as Baseline. VG-E2E applies the full vendor-recommended
deployment configuration, including native input/output formats, preprocessing,
runtime execution, and postprocessing. With this design, VG-NPU captures the
controlled effect of model transformation, whereas VG-E2E measures the per-
formance of the final vendor-guided deployment.

3

Following the proposed evaluation methodology, we analyze three research
questions using four NPUs and three vision workloads: ResNet50, YOLOv5m,
and YOLOv8s-pose. First, under VG-NPU, both latency and accuracy improve
in 10 of the 12 NPU–workload combinations. In contrast, under VG-E2E, System-
level latency decreases in all combinations, while accuracy decreases in eight.
This result shows that vendor-guided optimization can improve both metrics at
the controlled model-transformation level, but that lower latency in the final
deployment does not necessarily imply preserved accuracy.


Second, when comparing three NPUs on the same host, the relative perfor-
mance ranking among NPUs remains unchanged for YOLOv5m and YOLOv8s-
pose, but changes for ResNet50. This indicates that NPU-only performance does
not, in general, reliably predict actual end-to-end performance, and that the re-
lationship is workload-dependent.


Third, VG-E2E achieves lower System-level latency than VG-NPU in all
combinations. This suggests that deployment-level processing can provide ad-
ditional performance gains, while also indicating that such gains should not be
attributed to any single optimization component. Overall, these results show
that Edge NPU performance should be evaluated separately at the NPU-level
optimization and final deployment levels, rather than being treated as a single
performance metric.


The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related
work. Section 3 describes the three experimental configurations, workloads, NPU
platforms, and measurement methodology. Section 4 presents the main exper-
imental results and discusses the limitations of the study. Finally, Section 5
concludes the paper and outlines directions for future work.

2 Related Work

Benchmarking methodology and evaluation metrics: MLPerf Inference [12]
standardizes workloads, accuracy targets, execution scenarios, and measurement
rules to enable fair and reproducible comparisons of ML inference systems across
diverse hardware and software platforms. MLPerf Tiny [3] extends this bench-
marking approach to ultra-low-power TinyML environments by jointly measur-
ing latency, energy, and accuracy. Its modular benchmark design also enables
the contributions of different layers of the deployment stack, including models,
frameworks, and hardware, to be analyzed separately. These efforts demonstrate
that, even across substantially different application domains, fair evaluation of
accuracy–latency–energy trade-offs requires considering multiple performance
metrics and separating the contributions of individual system layers.


Sze et al. [13] similarly emphasize that DNN inference systems should be
evaluated using multiple metrics, including accuracy, latency/throughput, en-
ergy/power, and hardware cost, and that performance should be measured un-
der representative workloads and runtime conditions. Coleman et al. [5] proposed
DAWNBench, highlighting the need for end-to-end system evaluation that cap-

tures the combined effects of model architecture, optimization procedures, soft-
ware frameworks, and hardware.


Following these evaluation principles, this study distinguishes controlled NPU-
only execution from native end-to-end deployment to isolate and analyze the
effects of vendor-guided optimization.


NPU/system-level and E2E performance analysis: Millar et al. [11]
compared microcontroller-scale µNPUs under common workloads and measure-
ment conditions, decomposing execution time into initialization, memory I/O,
inference, and post-processing to identify end-to-end performance bottlenecks.


Buch et al. [4] characterized the overheads beyond model inference in mo-
bile AI—including data capture, pre/post-processing, framework, and offloading
overheads—as the “AI tax,” and analyzed their impact on application-level end-
to-end performance.


Szegedi et al. [14] separately measured preprocessing, inference, and post-
processing for classification and detection models on edge GPUs, and compared
performance across frameworks, implementation languages, and precision set-
tings, demonstrating the need to consider both model inference time and total
processing time.


Kang et al. [9] showed that, in accelerator-based visual analytics systems, pre-
processing operations such as image decoding and resizing can become through-
put bottlenecks that are more significant than model inference itself.


Ham et al. [6], through their work on NNStreamer, demonstrated that ex-
ecution configuration can substantially affect the performance of on-device AI
pipelines composed of multiple processing stages. By connecting neural network
inference and data processing through GStreamer and comparing sequential ex-
ecution with stream-pipelined execution, they showed that the organization of
data flow and parallel execution affects overall latency, throughput, and resource
utilization.


While these studies demonstrate the importance of system-level overheads
beyond NPU inference, our work distinguishes vendor optimization on commer-
cial Edge NPUs into NPU-only model transformation and full deployment, and
compares the performance impact at each level.


Optimization/toolchain effects: EdgeMark [7] proposed a benchmarking
system that automates model generation, optimization, conversion, and deploy-
ment for embedded AI tools, enabling multiple toolchains to be compared under
consistent conditions.


Ahn et al. [1] compared INT8/FP16 and static/dynamic quantization across
different frameworks and edge hardware, showing that the effectiveness of the
same model optimization can vary depending on software frameworks and hard-
ware support. Baciu et al. [2] similarly compared porting frameworks and quanti-
zation configurations on real MCUs, showing that model quantization can reduce
model size and classification time at the cost of reduced accuracy.


Ulker et al. [15] showed that inference performance depends on both the
computational structure of a model and framework-specific operator implemen-

tations, while MLonMCU [10] demonstrated that inference performance and the
gains from auto-tuning can vary with TVM schedules and data layouts.


In contrast to these studies, our work does not focus on comparing indi-
vidual quantization techniques or deployment tools. Instead, we analyze how
complete vendor-recommended optimization recipes affect controlled NPU-only
performance and actual end-to-end deployment performance, considering both
accuracy and latency.

3 Benchmark Design

To distinguish the effects of vendor-provided NPU optimizations on accuracy
and latency between model transformation and final deployment, we define three
benchmark configurations: Baseline, Vendor-Guided NPU-Only (VG-NPU), and
Vendor-Guided End-to-End (VG-E2E). By comparing Baseline and VG-NPU,
we examine the changes introduced by vendor-guided model transformation,
while VG-E2E is used to evaluate the final performance of the full vendor-
recommended deployment configuration. In Fig. 1, we illustrate the three con-
figurations, the execution paths, and the corresponding latency measurement
methodology.

3.1 Benchmark Framework

Fig. 1. Execution paths and latency measurement intervals of the benchmark frame-
work. Baseline and VG-NPU use the same execution path, whereas VG-E2E follows the
vendor-guided deployment pipeline. Runtime-call latency measures the elapsed time of
the runtime API invocation, which includes NPU execution and any overhead incurred
within the runtime call, while System-level latency measures the total execution time
from image input to final prediction.

Fig. 1 illustrates the execution paths of the three benchmark configurations.
Baseline and VG-NPU use the same benchmark framework and generate the final
prediction through identical preprocessing, NPU runtime invocation, and post-
processing steps. The two configurations are also designed to use the same model

inputs and outputs. The primary difference between Baseline and VG-NPU is
the model transformation configuration used to generate the NPU-executable
model. In contrast, VG-E2E uses the vendor-recommended deployment pipeline,
including native input/output formats, preprocessing, runtime, and postprocess-
ing. Accuracy is evaluated using the same evaluator for all configurations.


Runtime-call latency measures the runtime API invocation, while System-
level latency measures the time from image loading to final prediction. Since
Baseline and VG-NPU use the same runtime interface, their model-transformation
effects are compared using Runtime-call latency. Overall deployment perfor-
mance, including VG-E2E, is compared using System-level latency.


All experiments use synchronous single-stream execution with batch size 1
and the same 5,000-image evaluation set. After 10 warm-up runs, the full set is
executed four times. We take the median latency per image across the four runs
and report the mean over all 5,000 images.

3.3 Workloads and Datasets


To account for the possibility that NPU optimization effects vary with work-
load computation and output-processing characteristics, we select ResNet50,
YOLOv5m, and YOLOv8s-pose to represent image classification, object detec-
tion, and pose estimation, respectively.


ResNet50 represents image classification, YOLOv5m object detection, and
YOLOv8s-pose human pose estimation. Accuracy is evaluated based on the final
semantic predictions. For Baseline and VG-NPU, identical model outputs and
a common postprocessing pipeline are used so that differences in NPU-specific
output tensor layouts do not affect the comparison. For the YOLO workloads,
decoding, confidence filtering, and NMS are performed using the same common
postprocessor across all NPUs. Detailed output tensor configurations and the
threshold settings used for accuracy and latency measurements are provided in
the extended technical report [8].

3.4 Vendor-Specific Deployment Configuration


For each NPU, we apply the optimization and deployment configurations recom-
mended by the corresponding vendor, including quantization, precision, graph
transformation, preprocessing/postprocessing, and runtime pipeline.


– Specifically, Hailo uses optimization/compression-level tuning, mixed preci-

runtime pipelines. Detailed model-specific options and exceptional settings are

4.2 RQ2: Does NPU-only performance predict end-to-end
performance?


To examine whether NPU-only performance can predict actual end-to-end per-
formance, we compare the relative performance rankings among NPUs using
VG-NPU Runtime-call latency and VG-E2E System-level latency. To minimize
the effect of host differences, we focus on Hailo-8, Hailo-10H, and DeepX DX-M1,
all measured on the same Jetson Orin Nano host. Mobilint Regulus is excluded
from this comparison because it was measured on a separate vendor-provided
Regulus SOM.


For ResNet50, the performance ranking differs between NPU-only and end-
to-end measurements. Under VG-NPU, Runtime-call latency follows Hailo-8 <
Hailo-10H < DeepX DX-M1, whereas under VG-E2E, System-level latency fol-
lows DeepX DX-M1 < Hailo-8 < Hailo-10H. Notably, DeepX DX-M1, which is
the slowest in the NPU-only measurement, achieves the lowest E2E latency un-
der VG-E2E. This shows that NPU inference performance alone does not always
predict overall deployment performance.


In contrast, for YOLOv5m and YOLOv8s-pose, the relative ranking among
NPUs remains unchanged across the two measurements. For both workloads, the
ranking is Hailo-8 < Hailo-10H < DeepX DX-M1 for both VG-NPU Runtime-call
latency and VG-E2E System-level latency. These results show that the relation-
ship between NPU-only and end-to-end performance is workload-dependent, and
that overall system performance can be influenced not only by NPU inference but
also by preprocessing, postprocessing, and vendor-specific execution pipelines.

4.3 RQ3: How much additional benefit comes from vendor-guided
deployment?


To examine whether vendor-guided deployment provides additional performance
gains beyond NPU-level optimization, we compare the System-level latency of

VG-NPU and VG-E2E. VG-E2E achieves lower latency than VG-NPU in all 12
NPU–workload combinations, with reductions ranging from 10.4% to 70.7%.
Particularly large additional improvements are observed for YOLOv5m and
YOLOv8s-pose on Hailo-10H, all three workloads on DeepX DX-M1, and YOLOv8s-
pose on Mobilint Regulus.


VG-NPU and VG-E2E apply the same vendor-guided model transformation,
but VG-E2E additionally uses vendor-specific preprocessing, postprocessing, and
runtime pipelines. Since VG-E2E achieves lower E2E latency than VG-NPU
in all combinations, the additional latency gains can be attributed to system-
level processing beyond NPU-internal model transformation. This suggests that
deployment-level optimization plays an important role in further reducing overall
latency. However, because multiple components are changed simultaneously, the
observed gains cannot be isolated as the effect of any single preprocessing or
postprocessing technique.

4.4 Limitations

This study is limited to four NPUs, three vision workloads, specific software
stacks, and synchronous batch-1 execution, and does not explore all compiler
and quantization configurations. In Baseline and VG-NPU, some full-graph op-
timizations are restricted to preserve identical model inputs, outputs, and host-
side processing. In VG-E2E, multiple deployment components change simul-
taneously, preventing us from isolating the effect of individual optimizations.
Because some platforms use different hosts, absolute E2E latency cannot be
attributed solely to NPU performance. Power and energy-efficiency evaluation
was excluded because the available power telemetry interfaces and measurement
coverage differed across platforms, making it difficult to establish a consistent
power measurement interval. Consequently, we cannot determine whether the
observed latency improvements translate into better power efficiency or lower
energy per inference. Thus, our results should be interpreted as the observed ef-
fects in vendor-guided optimization within the scope of our experiments, rather
than as maximum achievable performance or universal superiority.

5 Conclusion and Future Work

Using four commercial Edge NPUs and three widely used vision workloads span-
ning image classification, object detection, and pose estimation, our findings
show that Edge NPU performance should be interpreted by distinguishing NPU-
level model transformation from final deployment, rather than treating infer-
ence performance as a single metric. First, vendor-guided model transformation
generally reduces NPU inference latency while preserving accuracy under fixed
model inputs, outputs, and host-side processing. Second, such NPU-level im-
provements do not always translate directly into final End-to-End performance;
for some workloads, the relative performance ranking among NPUs changes after

rather than NPU execution alone.


Future work will extend the evaluation to a broader range of NPUs and work-

Benchmarking Vendor-Guided Optimizations on
Edge NPUs: From NPU Only to End-to-End
Performance

Youngjin Jo1,2[0009−0000−8772−5837], Jihwan Kim1[0009−0000−3446−4805], Minseok
Choi1[0009−0003−6346−4144], Kwanghoon Choi1[0000−0003−3519−3650], Jusung
Kang2[0000−0002−7908−9452], and Jaein Kim2[0009−0006−0739−9052]

1 Chonnam National University, Gwangju, 61186, Korea
{jo.youngjin,213652,213837,kwanghoon.choi}@jnu.ac.kr
2 Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute, Gwangju, 61012, Korea
{k92492,jaein}@etri.re.kr

Abstract. Edge NPU performance depends not only on hardware ca-
pabilities, but also on model transformation and the overall deployment
pipeline. We propose a benchmarking methodology that separates these
effects by comparing three configurations: Baseline, Vendor Guided NPU
Only (VG-NPU), and Vendor Guided End-to-End (VG-E2E), where VG-
NPU preserves common model I/O and host-side processing while VG-
E2E follows the vendor-native deployment pipeline. We apply this method-
ology to four edge NPUs and three vision workloads. VG-NPU improves
both accuracy and runtime-call latency in 10 of 12 NPU–workload com-
binations, whereas VG-E2E reduces System-level latency in all combina-
tions but improves accuracy in only four. Moreover, NPU-level perfor-
mance rankings do not always match End-to-End rankings, and VG-
E2E provides an additional 10.4–70.7% reduction in System-level la-
tency over VG-NPU. These results demonstrate the importance of eval-
uating vendor-guided optimization separately at the controlled model-
transformation and full deployment levels.

# Keywords: Edge NPU · Benchmarking · Vendor-Guided Optimization
· Inference Performance · End-to-End Evaluation

1 Introduction

As AI deployment expands, efficient inference has become increasingly impor-
tant, particularly in mobile and edge environments with tight power and resource
constraints. Neural Processing Units (NPUs) address this demand by accelerat-
ing tensor operations commonly used in neural networks, often providing higher
efficiency than general-purpose CPUs and GPUs for supported workloads [13].
In practice, however, NPU inference performance depends not only on hard-
ware compute capability, but also on the surrounding software stack, including
operator support, compiler optimizations, quantization, runtime execution, and
input/output processing.

2 Youngjin Jo et al.

Evaluating NPU-based inference systems requires considering both accuracy
and latency. Accuracy reflects how well the predictive quality of the original
model is preserved during deployment to an NPU, while latency measures the
execution time required to produce the final prediction from an input. In particu-
lar, latency can differ substantially depending on whether it measures only NPU
inference or end-to-end execution including preprocessing and postprocessing.
This study focuses on how accuracy and latency change across the deployment
pipelines of different NPUs.

Comparing different NPUs fairly is challenging. NPUs differ not only in hard-
ware architecture and supported operators, but also in their compilers, quantiza-
tion policies, precision settings, runtime interfaces, and preprocessing/postprocessing
pipelines. Consequently, even when starting from the same source model, apply-
ing vendor-recommended model transformations and deployment recipes can
change not only the final executable model, but also which operations are exe-
cuted on the NPU and how the overall deployment pipeline is constructed. As
a result, comparing only the final end-to-end (E2E) performance reported for
each vendor makes it difficult to determine whether an observed performance
difference arises from model transformations performed for NPU execution or
from the broader deployment pipeline, including preprocessing, postprocessing,
and runtime overheads.

Prior work has proposed benchmarking methodologies and evaluation met-
rics for fair comparison of ML inference systems [13, 12], and has analyzed how
preprocessing, postprocessing, framework, and runtime overheads beyond model
inference affect end-to-end performance [11, 4]. Other studies have shown that
the execution performance of the same model can vary depending on quan-
tization, compilers, deployment tools, and hardware-specific optimizations [7,
1]. However, these studies have primarily focused on cross-platform comparison,
system-level overheads, or the effects of individual optimization techniques. They
have not explicitly separated the effect of vendor-guided optimization into two
levels: model transformation under fixed model inputs, outputs, and host-side
processing, and actual vendor-native end-to-end deployment. By distinguishing
these two levels, this study separately examines how model transformation and
full deployment affect accuracy and latency.

To investigate this research gap, we define three experimental conditions:
Baseline, Vendor-Guided NPU-Only (VG-NPU), and Vendor-Guided End-to-
End (VG-E2E). Baseline serves as a reference configuration that permits only
the transformations required for NPU execution while limiting optional vendor-
specific optimizations. VG-NPU applies the vendor-guided model transforma-
tion recipe while preserving the same model inputs and outputs and the same
host-side processing as Baseline. VG-E2E applies the full vendor-recommended
deployment configuration, including native input/output formats, preprocessing,
runtime execution, and postprocessing. With this design, VG-NPU captures the
controlled effect of model transformation, whereas VG-E2E measures the per-
formance of the final vendor-guided deployment.

Benchmarking Vendor-Guided Optimizations on Edge NPUs

3

Following the proposed evaluation methodology, we analyze three research
questions using four NPUs and three vision workloads: ResNet50, YOLOv5m,
and YOLOv8s-pose. First, under VG-NPU, both latency and accuracy improve
in 10 of the 12 NPU–workload combinations. In contrast, under VG-E2E, System-
level latency decreases in all combinations, while accuracy decreases in eight.
This result shows that vendor-guided optimization can improve both metrics at
the controlled model-transformation level, but that lower latency in the final
deployment does not necessarily imply preserved accuracy.

Second, when comparing three NPUs on the same host, the relative perfor-
mance ranking among NPUs remains unchanged for YOLOv5m and YOLOv8s-
pose, but changes for ResNet50. This indicates that NPU-only performance does
not, in general, reliably predict actual end-to-end performance, and that the re-
lationship is workload-dependent.

Third, VG-E2E achieves lower System-level latency than VG-NPU in all
combinations. This suggests that deployment-level processing can provide ad-
ditional performance gains, while also indicating that such gains should not be
attributed to any single optimization component. Overall, these results show
that Edge NPU performance should be evaluated separately at the NPU-level
optimization and final deployment levels, rather than being treated as a single
performance metric.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related
work. Section 3 describes the three experimental configurations, workloads, NPU
platforms, and measurement methodology. Section 4 presents the main exper-
imental results and discusses the limitations of the study. Finally, Section 5
concludes the paper and outlines directions for future work.

# 2 Related Work

Benchmarking methodology and evaluation metrics: MLPerf Inference [12]
standardizes workloads, accuracy targets, execution scenarios, and measurement
rules to enable fair and reproducible comparisons of ML inference systems across
diverse hardware and software platforms. MLPerf Tiny [3] extends this bench-
marking approach to ultra-low-power TinyML environments by jointly measur-
ing latency, energy, and accuracy. Its modular benchmark design also enables
the contributions of different layers of the deployment stack, including models,
frameworks, and hardware, to be analyzed separately. These efforts demonstrate
that, even across substantially different application domains, fair evaluation of
accuracy–latency–energy trade-offs requires considering multiple performance
metrics and separating the contributions of individual system layers.

Sze et al. [13] similarly emphasize that DNN inference systems should be
evaluated using multiple metrics, including accuracy, latency/throughput, en-
ergy/power, and hardware cost, and that performance should be measured un-
der representative workloads and runtime conditions. Coleman et al. [5] proposed
DAWNBench, highlighting the need for end-to-end system evaluation that cap-

4 Youngjin Jo et al.

tures the combined effects of model architecture, optimization procedures, soft-
ware frameworks, and hardware.

Following these evaluation principles, this study distinguishes controlled NPU-
only execution from native end-to-end deployment to isolate and analyze the
effects of vendor-guided optimization.

NPU/system-level and E2E performance analysis: Millar et al. [11]
compared microcontroller-scale µNPUs under common workloads and measure-
ment conditions, decomposing execution time into initialization, memory I/O,
inference, and post-processing to identify end-to-end performance bottlenecks.

Buch et al. [4] characterized the overheads beyond model inference in mo-
bile AI—including data capture, pre/post-processing, framework, and offloading
overheads—as the “AI tax,” and analyzed their impact on application-level end-
to-end performance.

Szegedi et al. [14] separately measured preprocessing, inference, and post-
processing for classification and detection models on edge GPUs, and compared
performance across frameworks, implementation languages, and precision set-
tings, demonstrating the need to consider both model inference time and total
processing time.

Kang et al. [9] showed that, in accelerator-based visual analytics systems, pre-
processing operations such as image decoding and resizing can become through-
put bottlenecks that are more significant than model inference itself.

Ham et al. [6], through their work on NNStreamer, demonstrated that ex-
ecution configuration can substantially affect the performance of on-device AI
pipelines composed of multiple processing stages. By connecting neural network
inference and data processing through GStreamer and comparing sequential ex-
ecution with stream-pipelined execution, they showed that the organization of
data flow and parallel execution affects overall latency, throughput, and resource
utilization.

While these studies demonstrate the importance of system-level overheads
beyond NPU inference, our work distinguishes vendor optimization on commer-
cial Edge NPUs into NPU-only model transformation and full deployment, and
compares the performance impact at each level.

Optimization/toolchain effects: EdgeMark [7] proposed a benchmarking
system that automates model generation, optimization, conversion, and deploy-
ment for embedded AI tools, enabling multiple toolchains to be compared under
consistent conditions.

Ahn et al. [1] compared INT8/FP16 and static/dynamic quantization across
different frameworks and edge hardware, showing that the effectiveness of the
same model optimization can vary depending on software frameworks and hard-
ware support. Baciu et al. [2] similarly compared porting frameworks and quanti-
zation configurations on real MCUs, showing that model quantization can reduce
model size and classification time at the cost of reduced accuracy.

Ulker et al. [15] showed that inference performance depends on both the
computational structure of a model and framework-specific operator implemen-

tations, while MLonMCU [10] demonstrated that inference performance and the
gains from auto-tuning can vary with TVM schedules and data layouts.

In contrast to these studies, our work does not focus on comparing indi-
vidual quantization techniques or deployment tools. Instead, we analyze how
complete vendor-recommended optimization recipes affect controlled NPU-only
performance and actual end-to-end deployment performance, considering both
accuracy and latency.

# 3 Benchmark Design

To distinguish the effects of vendor-provided NPU optimizations on accuracy
and latency between model transformation and final deployment, we define three
benchmark configurations: Baseline, Vendor-Guided NPU-Only (VG-NPU), and
Vendor-Guided End-to-End (VG-E2E). By comparing Baseline and VG-NPU,
we examine the changes introduced by vendor-guided model transformation,
while VG-E2E is used to evaluate the final performance of the full vendor-
recommended deployment configuration. In Fig. 1, we illustrate the three con-
figurations, the execution paths, and the corresponding latency measurement
methodology.

4.2 RQ2: Does NPU-only performance predict end-to-end
performance?

To examine whether NPU-only performance can predict actual end-to-end per-
formance, we compare the relative performance rankings among NPUs using
VG-NPU Runtime-call latency and VG-E2E System-level latency. To minimize
the effect of host differences, we focus on Hailo-8, Hailo-10H, and DeepX DX-M1,
all measured on the same Jetson Orin Nano host. Mobilint Regulus is excluded
from this comparison because it was measured on a separate vendor-provided
Regulus SOM.

For ResNet50, the performance ranking differs between NPU-only and end-
to-end measurements. Under VG-NPU, Runtime-call latency follows Hailo-8 <
Hailo-10H < DeepX DX-M1, whereas under VG-E2E, System-level latency fol-
lows DeepX DX-M1 < Hailo-8 < Hailo-10H. Notably, DeepX DX-M1, which is
the slowest in the NPU-only measurement, achieves the lowest E2E latency un-
der VG-E2E. This shows that NPU inference performance alone does not always
predict overall deployment performance.

In contrast, for YOLOv5m and YOLOv8s-pose, the relative ranking among
NPUs remains unchanged across the two measurements. For both workloads, the
ranking is Hailo-8 < Hailo-10H < DeepX DX-M1 for both VG-NPU Runtime-call
latency and VG-E2E System-level latency. These results show that the relation-
ship between NPU-only and end-to-end performance is workload-dependent, and
that overall system performance can be influenced not only by NPU inference but
also by preprocessing, postprocessing, and vendor-specific execution pipelines.

4.3 RQ3: How much additional benefit comes from vendor-guided
deployment?

To examine whether vendor-guided deployment provides additional performance
gains beyond NPU-level optimization, we compare the System-level latency of

VG-NPU and VG-E2E. VG-E2E achieves lower latency than VG-NPU in all 12
NPU–workload combinations, with reductions ranging from 10.4% to 70.7%.
Particularly large additional improvements are observed for YOLOv5m and
YOLOv8s-pose on Hailo-10H, all three workloads on DeepX DX-M1, and YOLOv8s-
pose on Mobilint Regulus.

VG-NPU and VG-E2E apply the same vendor-guided model transformation,
but VG-E2E additionally uses vendor-specific preprocessing, postprocessing, and
runtime pipelines. Since VG-E2E achieves lower E2E latency than VG-NPU
in all combinations, the additional latency gains can be attributed to system-
level processing beyond NPU-internal model transformation. This suggests that
deployment-level optimization plays an important role in further reducing overall
latency. However, because multiple components are changed simultaneously, the
observed gains cannot be isolated as the effect of any single preprocessing or
postprocessing technique.

4.4 Limitations

This study is limited to four NPUs, three vision workloads, specific software
stacks, and synchronous batch-1 execution, and does not explore all compiler
and quantization configurations. In Baseline and VG-NPU, some full-graph op-
timizations are restricted to preserve identical model inputs, outputs, and host-
side processing. In VG-E2E, multiple deployment components change simul-
taneously, preventing us from isolating the effect of individual optimizations.
Because some platforms use different hosts, absolute E2E latency cannot be
attributed solely to NPU performance. Power and energy-efficiency evaluation
was excluded because the available power telemetry interfaces and measurement
coverage differed across platforms, making it difficult to establish a consistent
power measurement interval. Consequently, we cannot determine whether the
observed latency improvements translate into better power efficiency or lower
energy per inference. Thus, our results should be interpreted as the observed ef-
fects in vendor-guided optimization within the scope of our experiments, rather
than as maximum achievable performance or universal superiority.

5 Conclusion and Future Work

Using four commercial Edge NPUs and three widely used vision workloads span-
ning image classification, object detection, and pose estimation, our findings
show that Edge NPU performance should be interpreted by distinguishing NPU-
level model transformation from final deployment, rather than treating infer-
ence performance as a single metric. First, vendor-guided model transformation
generally reduces NPU inference latency while preserving accuracy under fixed
model inputs, outputs, and host-side processing. Second, such NPU-level im-
provements do not always translate directly into final End-to-End performance;
for some workloads, the relative performance ranking among NPUs changes after

full deployment. Third, vendor-native deployment provides additional System-
level latency reductions across all evaluated combinations, but these performance
gains do not always preserve accuracy. These findings suggest that comparing
Edge NPUs requires considering the latency–accuracy trade-off jointly shaped
by model transformation, preprocessing, postprocessing, and runtime pipelines,
rather than NPU execution alone.

Future work will extend the evaluation to a broader range of NPUs and work-
loads, isolate the effects of individual optimizations, and incorporate workload-
specific accuracy constraints to better understand the sources of these trade-offs.

Edge NPUs: From NPU Only to End-to-End
Performance

Choi1[0009−0003−6346−4144], Kwanghoon Choi1[0000−0003−3519−3650], Jusung

Abstract. Edge NPU performance depends not only on hardware ca-
pabilities, but also on model transformation and the overall deployment
pipeline. We propose a benchmarking methodology that separates these
effects by comparing three configurations: Baseline, Vendor Guided NPU
Only (VG-NPU), and Vendor Guided End-to-End (VG-E2E), where VG-
NPU preserves common model I/O and host-side processing while VG-
E2E follows the vendor-native deployment pipeline. We apply this method-
ology to four edge NPUs and three vision workloads. VG-NPU improves
both accuracy and runtime-call latency in 10 of 12 NPU–workload com-
binations, whereas VG-E2E reduces System-level latency in all combina-
tions but improves accuracy in only four. Moreover, NPU-level perfor-
mance rankings do not always match End-to-End rankings, and VG-
E2E provides an additional 10.4–70.7% reduction in System-level la-
tency over VG-NPU. These results demonstrate the importance of eval-
uating vendor-guided optimization separately at the controlled model-
transformation and full deployment levels.
Keywords: Edge NPU · Benchmarking · Vendor-Guided Optimization
· Inference Performance · End-to-End Evaluation
1 Introduction
As AI deployment expands, efficient inference has become increasingly impor-
tant, particularly in mobile and edge environments with tight power and resource
constraints. Neural Processing Units (NPUs) address this demand by accelerat-
ing tensor operations commonly used in neural networks, often providing higher
efficiency than general-purpose CPUs and GPUs for supported workloads [13].
In practice, however, NPU inference performance depends not only on hard-
ware compute capability, but also on the surrounding software stack, including
operator support, compiler optimizations, quantization, runtime execution, and
input/output processing.
2 Youngjin Jo et al.
Evaluating NPU-based inference systems requires considering both accuracy
and latency. Accuracy reflects how well the predictive quality of the original
model is preserved during deployment to an NPU, while latency measures the
execution time required to produce the final prediction from an input. In particu-
lar, latency can differ substantially depending on whether it measures only NPU
inference or end-to-end execution including preprocessing and postprocessing.
This study focuses on how accuracy and latency change across the deployment
pipelines of different NPUs.
Comparing different NPUs fairly is challenging. NPUs differ not only in hard-
ware architecture and supported operators, but also in their compilers, quantiza-
tion policies, precision settings, runtime interfaces, and preprocessing/postprocessing
pipelines. Consequently, even when starting from the same source model, apply-
ing vendor-recommended model transformations and deployment recipes can
change not only the final executable model, but also which operations are exe-
cuted on the NPU and how the overall deployment pipeline is constructed. As
a result, comparing only the final end-to-end (E2E) performance reported for
each vendor makes it difficult to determine whether an observed performance
difference arises from model transformations performed for NPU execution or
from the broader deployment pipeline, including preprocessing, postprocessing,
and runtime overheads.
Prior work has proposed benchmarking methodologies and evaluation met-
rics for fair comparison of ML inference systems [13, 12], and has analyzed how
preprocessing, postprocessing, framework, and runtime overheads beyond model
inference affect end-to-end performance [11, 4]. Other studies have shown that
the execution performance of the same model can vary depending on quan-
tization, compilers, deployment tools, and hardware-specific optimizations [7,
1]. However, these studies have primarily focused on cross-platform comparison,
system-level overheads, or the effects of individual optimization techniques. They
have not explicitly separated the effect of vendor-guided optimization into two
levels: model transformation under fixed model inputs, outputs, and host-side
processing, and actual vendor-native end-to-end deployment. By distinguishing
these two levels, this study separately examines how model transformation and
full deployment affect accuracy and latency.
To investigate this research gap, we define three experimental conditions:
Baseline, Vendor-Guided NPU-Only (VG-NPU), and Vendor-Guided End-to-
End (VG-E2E). Baseline serves as a reference configuration that permits only
the transformations required for NPU execution while limiting optional vendor-
specific optimizations. VG-NPU applies the vendor-guided model transforma-
tion recipe while preserving the same model inputs and outputs and the same
host-side processing as Baseline. VG-E2E applies the full vendor-recommended
deployment configuration, including native input/output formats, preprocessing,
runtime execution, and postprocessing. With this design, VG-NPU captures the
controlled effect of model transformation, whereas VG-E2E measures the per-
formance of the final vendor-guided deployment.
Benchmarking Vendor-Guided Optimizations on Edge NPUs
3
Following the proposed evaluation methodology, we analyze three research
questions using four NPUs and three vision workloads: ResNet50, YOLOv5m,
and YOLOv8s-pose. First, under VG-NPU, both latency and accuracy improve
in 10 of the 12 NPU–workload combinations. In contrast, under VG-E2E, System-
level latency decreases in all combinations, while accuracy decreases in eight.
This result shows that vendor-guided optimization can improve both metrics at
the controlled model-transformation level, but that lower latency in the final
deployment does not necessarily imply preserved accuracy.
Second, when comparing three NPUs on the same host, the relative perfor-
mance ranking among NPUs remains unchanged for YOLOv5m and YOLOv8s-
pose, but changes for ResNet50. This indicates that NPU-only performance does
not, in general, reliably predict actual end-to-end performance, and that the re-
lationship is workload-dependent.
Third, VG-E2E achieves lower System-level latency than VG-NPU in all
combinations. This suggests that deployment-level processing can provide ad-
ditional performance gains, while also indicating that such gains should not be
attributed to any single optimization component. Overall, these results show
that Edge NPU performance should be evaluated separately at the NPU-level
optimization and final deployment levels, rather than being treated as a single
performance metric.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related
work. Section 3 describes the three experimental configurations, workloads, NPU
platforms, and measurement methodology. Section 4 presents the main exper-
imental results and discusses the limitations of the study. Finally, Section 5
concludes the paper and outlines directions for future work.
2 Related Work
Benchmarking methodology and evaluation metrics: MLPerf Inference [12]
standardizes workloads, accuracy targets, execution scenarios, and measurement
rules to enable fair and reproducible comparisons of ML inference systems across
diverse hardware and software platforms. MLPerf Tiny [3] extends this bench-
marking approach to ultra-low-power TinyML environments by jointly measur-
ing latency, energy, and accuracy. Its modular benchmark design also enables
the contributions of different layers of the deployment stack, including models,
frameworks, and hardware, to be analyzed separately. These efforts demonstrate
that, even across substantially different application domains, fair evaluation of
accuracy–latency–energy trade-offs requires considering multiple performance
metrics and separating the contributions of individual system layers.
Sze et al. [13] similarly emphasize that DNN inference systems should be
evaluated using multiple metrics, including accuracy, latency/throughput, en-
ergy/power, and hardware cost, and that performance should be measured un-
der representative workloads and runtime conditions. Coleman et al. [5] proposed
DAWNBench, highlighting the need for end-to-end system evaluation that cap-
4 Youngjin Jo et al.
tures the combined effects of model architecture, optimization procedures, soft-
ware frameworks, and hardware.
Following these evaluation principles, this study distinguishes controlled NPU-
only execution from native end-to-end deployment to isolate and analyze the
effects of vendor-guided optimization.
NPU/system-level and E2E performance analysis: Millar et al. [11]
compared microcontroller-scale µNPUs under common workloads and measure-
ment conditions, decomposing execution time into initialization, memory I/O,
inference, and post-processing to identify end-to-end performance bottlenecks.
Buch et al. [4] characterized the overheads beyond model inference in mo-
bile AI—including data capture, pre/post-processing, framework, and offloading
overheads—as the “AI tax,” and analyzed their impact on application-level end-
to-end performance.
Szegedi et al. [14] separately measured preprocessing, inference, and post-
processing for classification and detection models on edge GPUs, and compared
performance across frameworks, implementation languages, and precision set-
tings, demonstrating the need to consider both model inference time and total
processing time.
Kang et al. [9] showed that, in accelerator-based visual analytics systems, pre-
processing operations such as image decoding and resizing can become through-
put bottlenecks that are more significant than model inference itself.
Ham et al. [6], through their work on NNStreamer, demonstrated that ex-
ecution configuration can substantially affect the performance of on-device AI
pipelines composed of multiple processing stages. By connecting neural network
inference and data processing through GStreamer and comparing sequential ex-
ecution with stream-pipelined execution, they showed that the organization of
data flow and parallel execution affects overall latency, throughput, and resource
utilization.
While these studies demonstrate the importance of system-level overheads
beyond NPU inference, our work distinguishes vendor optimization on commer-
cial Edge NPUs into NPU-only model transformation and full deployment, and
compares the performance impact at each level.
Optimization/toolchain effects: EdgeMark [7] proposed a benchmarking
system that automates model generation, optimization, conversion, and deploy-
ment for embedded AI tools, enabling multiple toolchains to be compared under
consistent conditions.
Ahn et al. [1] compared INT8/FP16 and static/dynamic quantization across
different frameworks and edge hardware, showing that the effectiveness of the
same model optimization can vary depending on software frameworks and hard-
ware support. Baciu et al. [2] similarly compared porting frameworks and quanti-
zation configurations on real MCUs, showing that model quantization can reduce
model size and classification time at the cost of reduced accuracy.
Ulker et al. [15] showed that inference performance depends on both the
computational structure of a model and framework-specific operator implemen-

tations, while MLonMCU [10] demonstrated that inference performance and the
gains from auto-tuning can vary with TVM schedules and data layouts.
In contrast to these studies, our work does not focus on comparing indi-
vidual quantization techniques or deployment tools. Instead, we analyze how
complete vendor-recommended optimization recipes affect controlled NPU-only
performance and actual end-to-end deployment performance, considering both
accuracy and latency.
3 Benchmark Design
To distinguish the effects of vendor-provided NPU optimizations on accuracy
and latency between model transformation and final deployment, we define three
benchmark configurations: Baseline, Vendor-Guided NPU-Only (VG-NPU), and
Vendor-Guided End-to-End (VG-E2E). By comparing Baseline and VG-NPU,
we examine the changes introduced by vendor-guided model transformation,
while VG-E2E is used to evaluate the final performance of the full vendor-
recommended deployment configuration. In Fig. 1, we illustrate the three con-
figurations, the execution paths, and the corresponding latency measurement
methodology.

Runtime-call latency measures the runtime API invocation, while System-
level latency measures the time from image loading to final prediction. Since
Baseline and VG-NPU use the same runtime interface, their model-transformation
effects are compared using Runtime-call latency. Overall deployment perfor-
mance, including VG-E2E, is compared using System-level latency.
All experiments use synchronous single-stream execution with batch size 1
and the same 5,000-image evaluation set. After 10 warm-up runs, the full set is
executed four times. We take the median latency per image across the four runs
and report the mean over all 5,000 images.

The Baseline configuration serves as the reference point for evaluating the
effects of the two vendor-guided optimization configurations.
– Model conversion and INT8 post-training quantization are required to make
the model executable on each NPU, and these are also applied in the Baseline
configuration, since the original FP32 model cannot be executed directly on
the NPU without these transformations.

– In contrast, vendor-specific optimizations that are not required for model
execution are disabled in the Baseline configuration. These include fine-
tuning, mixed precision, weight compression, enhanced quantization, graph-
level performance optimization, and resource-allocation tuning. These op-
timizations are enabled only in the vendor-guided configurations, allowing
their effects on performance and accuracy to be measured relative to the
Baseline.
VG-E2E evaluates the deployment performance of the vendor-native execu-
tion path, including preprocessing, NPU inference, and postprocessing, using the
deployment modules and recommended model-transformation settings provided
by each vendor.
– Model transformation uses the vendor-recommended model graph, quanti-
zation, and compiler optimization settings, while execution uses native in-
put/output formats and vendor-specific preprocessing, runtime, and post-
processing.
– Therefore, changes observed under VG-E2E are interpreted as the effect of
the overall vendor-guided deployment rather than that of any single opti-
mization technique.
To isolate the effects of NPU inference and model transformation from the
overall E2E performance changes, we additionally define the VG-NPU configu-
ration.
– VG-NPU follows the same execution setup as Baseline, but applies the
vendor-recommended model-transformation recipe, including quantization
and compiler optimizations.
– Therefore, the performance difference between Baseline and VG-NPU cap-
tures the effect of vendor-recommended model transformation on NPU in-
ference.
3.3 Workloads and Datasets
To account for the possibility that NPU optimization effects vary with work-
load computation and output-processing characteristics, we select ResNet50,
YOLOv5m, and YOLOv8s-pose to represent image classification, object detec-
tion, and pose estimation, respectively.
ResNet50 represents image classification, YOLOv5m object detection, and
YOLOv8s-pose human pose estimation. Accuracy is evaluated based on the final
semantic predictions. For Baseline and VG-NPU, identical model outputs and
a common postprocessing pipeline are used so that differences in NPU-specific
output tensor layouts do not affect the comparison. For the YOLO workloads,
decoding, confidence filtering, and NMS are performed using the same common
postprocessor across all NPUs. Detailed output tensor configurations and the
threshold settings used for accuracy and latency measurements are provided in
the extended technical report [8].

3.4 Vendor-Specific Deployment Configuration
For each NPU, we apply the optimization and deployment configurations recom-
mended by the corresponding vendor, including quantization, precision, graph
transformation, preprocessing/postprocessing, and runtime pipeline.
– Specifically, Hailo uses optimization/compression-level tuning, mixed preci-
sion, and quantization fine-tuning, together with a GStreamer-based execu-
tion path and model-integrated normalization or NMS.
– DeepX applies compiler optimization levels and enhanced quantization, and
uses a DXSTREAM-based pipeline.
– Mobilint applies compiler optimization, percentile-based quantization, and
Hadamard transformation, using a Model Zoo- and qbruntime-based execu-
tion setup.
In VG-NPU, we primarily apply quantization and compiler-level model trans-
formations from these vendor settings, whereas VG-E2E additionally includes
vendor-native preprocessing, model-integrated processing, postprocessing, and
runtime pipelines. Detailed model-specific options and exceptional settings are
summarized in the extended technical report [8].

and accuracy, and how NPU-only performance translates into end-to-end per-

and accuracy?

4.2 RQ2: Does NPU-only performance predict end-to-end
performance?
To examine whether NPU-only performance can predict actual end-to-end per-
formance, we compare the relative performance rankings among NPUs using
VG-NPU Runtime-call latency and VG-E2E System-level latency. To minimize
the effect of host differences, we focus on Hailo-8, Hailo-10H, and DeepX DX-M1,
all measured on the same Jetson Orin Nano host. Mobilint Regulus is excluded
from this comparison because it was measured on a separate vendor-provided
Regulus SOM.
For ResNet50, the performance ranking differs between NPU-only and end-
to-end measurements. Under VG-NPU, Runtime-call latency follows Hailo-8 <
Hailo-10H < DeepX DX-M1, whereas under VG-E2E, System-level latency fol-
lows DeepX DX-M1 < Hailo-8 < Hailo-10H. Notably, DeepX DX-M1, which is
the slowest in the NPU-only measurement, achieves the lowest E2E latency un-
der VG-E2E. This shows that NPU inference performance alone does not always
predict overall deployment performance.
In contrast, for YOLOv5m and YOLOv8s-pose, the relative ranking among
NPUs remains unchanged across the two measurements. For both workloads, the
ranking is Hailo-8 < Hailo-10H < DeepX DX-M1 for both VG-NPU Runtime-call
latency and VG-E2E System-level latency. These results show that the relation-
ship between NPU-only and end-to-end performance is workload-dependent, and
that overall system performance can be influenced not only by NPU inference but
also by preprocessing, postprocessing, and vendor-specific execution pipelines.
4.3 RQ3: How much additional benefit comes from vendor-guided
deployment?
To examine whether vendor-guided deployment provides additional performance
gains beyond NPU-level optimization, we compare the System-level latency of
12 Youngjin Jo et al.
VG-NPU and VG-E2E. VG-E2E achieves lower latency than VG-NPU in all 12
NPU–workload combinations, with reductions ranging from 10.4% to 70.7%.
Particularly large additional improvements are observed for YOLOv5m and
YOLOv8s-pose on Hailo-10H, all three workloads on DeepX DX-M1, and YOLOv8s-
pose on Mobilint Regulus.
VG-NPU and VG-E2E apply the same vendor-guided model transformation,
but VG-E2E additionally uses vendor-specific preprocessing, postprocessing, and
runtime pipelines. Since VG-E2E achieves lower E2E latency than VG-NPU
in all combinations, the additional latency gains can be attributed to system-
level processing beyond NPU-internal model transformation. This suggests that
deployment-level optimization plays an important role in further reducing overall
latency. However, because multiple components are changed simultaneously, the
observed gains cannot be isolated as the effect of any single preprocessing or
postprocessing technique.
4.4 Limitations
This study is limited to four NPUs, three vision workloads, specific software
stacks, and synchronous batch-1 execution, and does not explore all compiler
and quantization configurations. In Baseline and VG-NPU, some full-graph op-
timizations are restricted to preserve identical model inputs, outputs, and host-
side processing. In VG-E2E, multiple deployment components change simul-
taneously, preventing us from isolating the effect of individual optimizations.
Because some platforms use different hosts, absolute E2E latency cannot be
attributed solely to NPU performance. Power and energy-efficiency evaluation
was excluded because the available power telemetry interfaces and measurement
coverage differed across platforms, making it difficult to establish a consistent
power measurement interval. Consequently, we cannot determine whether the
observed latency improvements translate into better power efficiency or lower
energy per inference. Thus, our results should be interpreted as the observed ef-
fects in vendor-guided optimization within the scope of our experiments, rather
than as maximum achievable performance or universal superiority.
5 Conclusion and Future Work
Using four commercial Edge NPUs and three widely used vision workloads span-
ning image classification, object detection, and pose estimation, our findings
show that Edge NPU performance should be interpreted by distinguishing NPU-
level model transformation from final deployment, rather than treating infer-
ence performance as a single metric. First, vendor-guided model transformation
generally reduces NPU inference latency while preserving accuracy under fixed
model inputs, outputs, and host-side processing. Second, such NPU-level im-
provements do not always translate directly into final End-to-End performance;
for some workloads, the relative performance ranking among NPUs changes after
Benchmarking Vendor-Guided Optimizations on Edge NPUs

full deployment. Third, vendor-native deployment provides additional System-
level latency reductions across all evaluated combinations, but these performance
gains do not always preserve accuracy. These findings suggest that comparing
Edge NPUs requires considering the latency–accuracy trade-off jointly shaped
by model transformation, preprocessing, postprocessing, and runtime pipelines,
rather than NPU execution alone.
Future work will extend the evaluation to a broader range of NPUs and work-
loads, isolate the effects of individual optimizations, and incorporate workload-
specific accuracy constraints to better understand the sources of these trade-offs.

Abstract. Edge NPU performance depends not only on hardware ca-
pabilities, but also on model transformation and the overall deployment
pipeline. We propose a benchmarking methodology that separates these
effects by comparing three configurations: Baseline, Vendor Guided NPU
Only (VG-NPU), and Vendor Guided End-to-End (VG-E2E), where VG-
NPU preserves common model I/O and host-side processing while VG-
E2E follows the vendor-native deployment pipeline. We apply this method-
ology to four edge NPUs and three vision workloads. VG-NPU improves
both accuracy and runtime-call latency in 10 of 12 NPU–workload com-
binations, whereas VG-E2E reduces System-level latency in all combina-
tions but improves accuracy in only four. Moreover, NPU-level perfor-
mance rankings do not always match End-to-End rankings, and VG-
E2E provides an additional 10.4–70.7% reduction in System-level la-
tency over VG-NPU. These results demonstrate the importance of eval-
uating vendor-guided optimization separately at the controlled model-
transformation and full deployment levels.

Abstract. Edge NPU performance depends not only on hardware ca-
pabilities, but also on model transformation and the overall deployment
pipeline. We propose a benchmarking methodology that separates these
effects by comparing three configurations: Baseline, Vendor Guided NPU
Only (VG-NPU), and Vendor Guided End-to-End (VG-E2E), where VG-
NPU preserves common model I/O and host-side processing while VG-
E2E follows the vendor-native deployment pipeline. We apply this method-
ology to four edge NPUs and three vision workloads. VG-NPU improves
both accuracy and runtime-call latency in 10 of 12 NPU–workload com-
binations, whereas VG-E2E reduces System-level latency in all combina-
tions but improves accuracy in only four. Moreover, NPU-level perfor-
mance rankings do not always match End-to-End rankings, and VG-
E2E provides an additional 10.4–70.7% reduction in System-level la-
tency over VG-NPU. These results demonstrate the importance of eval-
uating vendor-guided optimization separately at the controlled model-
transformation and full deployment levels.

Comparing different NPUs fairly is challenging. NPUs differ not only in hard-
ware architecture and supported operators, but also in their compilers, quantiza-
tion policies, precision settings, runtime interfaces, and preprocessing/postprocessing
pipelines. Consequently, even when starting from the same source model, apply-
ing vendor-recommended model transformations and deployment recipes can
change not only the final executable model, but also which operations are exe-
cuted on the NPU and how the overall deployment pipeline is constructed. As
a result, comparing only the final end-to-end (E2E) performance reported for
each vendor makes it difficult to determine whether an observed performance
difference arises from model transformations performed for NPU execution or
from the broader deployment pipeline, including preprocessing, postprocessing,
and runtime overheads.

To investigate this research gap, we define three experimental conditions:
Baseline, Vendor-Guided NPU-Only (VG-NPU), and Vendor-Guided End-to-

host-side processing as Baseline. VG-E2E applies the full vendor-recommended
deployment configuration, including native input/output formats, preprocessing,
runtime execution, and postprocessing. With this design, VG-NPU captures the
controlled effect of model transformation, whereas VG-E2E measures the per-
formance of the final vendor-guided deployment.

that, even across substantially different application domains, fair evaluation of
accuracy–latency–energy trade-offs requires considering multiple performance
metrics and separating the contributions of individual system layers.

content.html: 4.4 Limitations
content.markdown: 4.4 Limitations
content.text: 4.4 Limitations

content.html:
This study is limited to four NPUs, three vision workloads, specific software
stacks, and synchronous batch-1 execution, and does not explore all compiler
and quantization configurations. In Baseline and VG-NPU, some full-graph op-
timizations are restricted to preserve identical model inputs, outputs, and host-
side processing. In VG-E2E, multiple deployment components change simul-
taneously, preventing us from isolating the effect of individual optimizations.
Because some platforms use different hosts, absolute E2E latency cannot be
attributed solely to NPU performance. Power and energy-efficiency evaluation
was excluded because the available power telemetry interfaces and measurement
coverage differed across platforms, making it difficult to establish a consistent
power measurement interval. Consequently, we cannot determine whether the
observed latency improvements translate into better power efficiency or lower
energy per inference. Thus, our results should be interpreted as the observed ef-
fects in vendor-guided optimization within the scope of our experiments, rather
than as maximum achievable performance or universal superiority.
